Article Title: The 'troika' of Mumbai: 3 dons, 3 spheres, 1 city's underbelly
Article Text:
(L-R) Karim Lala, Haji Mastan and Varadarajan Mudaliar.

Who controlled what?

A 'Troika'

The old-school don

Zanjeer Movie Poster

The don who traded the gun for glamour

The real-life don behind ‘Nayakan’

Kamal Haasan in Nayakan.

The old order and its unwritten rules

Then came Dawood

The end of an era

Poll Vote & Share your view How do you feel about the portrayal of gang-related violence in modern media? It's glorified and inappropriate It's necessary for awareness It's just entertainment 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion





MUMBAI: Long before Dawood Ibrahim became synonymous with Mumbai's underworld, the city had already produced a generation of crime bosses who controlled smuggling routes, gambling dens, illicit liquor networks and local rackets.They were different from the gangsters who followed them.Their power was often rooted in particular neighbourhoods and communities and their influence extended beyond the criminal world into cinema, politics and local social networks.Among the most prominent were Karim Lala, Haji Mastan and Varadarajan Mudaliar — three men who, together, formed the old guard of Mumbai's underworld in the 1960s and 1970s.They were a troika that controlled the city's underworld during that period.Their era would eventually give way to a more violent phase. At the centre of that transformation was a young gangster from Dongri: Dawood Ibrahim.Abdul Karim Sher Khan, better known as Karim Lala, arrived in Mumbai from Afghanistan and began his life in the city around the docks.He gradually built a reputation by settling disputes and organising fellow Pathans before expanding into gambling and smuggling.Lala became involved in the smuggling of gold, silver and electronics and also operated gambling, drug and protection rackets.He was regarded as the first don of his kind in Mumbai and became the most prominent figure of the city's Pathan mafia.His influence was not confined to crime. Lala became an important figure among Mumbai's Pathan community and was known for his involvement in community affairs.By the 1960s and 1970s, he was part of a powerful trio with Haji Mastan and Varadarajan Mudaliar. The three operated largely in different spheres but collectively represented the old order of Mumbai's underworld.Lala's image eventually became so entrenched in popular culture that he was reported to have inspired Pran's Pathan character in Zanjeer.But the old order would not survive the arrival of a younger generation.Haji Mastan emerged from the same world of Mumbai's docks.Mastan arrived at the Bombay docks as a porter in 1944, where he met Karim Lala. He became a major player in the smuggling of precious metals between 1955 and 1975 and later developed close links with Bollywood, including financing film directors and studios.Unlike the image of the gun-toting gangster that would later dominate Mumbai's crime stories, Mastan cultivated a different public persona.He was known for his polished appearance, his connections with film personalities and his philanthropy. Yet that public image existed alongside his criminal activities.His reputation for helping the poor did not erase the criminality he practised, encouraged and condoned.Mastan's proximity to Bollywood became part of the mythology surrounding Mumbai's underworld.Both Karim Lala and Haji Mastan were seen socialising with film stars at parties in the 1970s, while Mastan even entered politics and floated his own political outfit.His influence was so strong that his life became associated with one of Hindi cinema's most famous gangster films.According to multiple reports, the popular movie 'Deewaar' was loosely based on Mastan's life, although the connection has also been disputed by his family.Then there was Varadarajan Mudaliar, who represented another strand of Mumbai's underworld.Mudaliar came to Mumbai from Tamil Nadu and initially worked as a porter. According to reports, he soon became involved in stealing dock cargo with Mastan's help.His influence grew particularly among Tamil migrants in central Mumbai.Unlike later gangsters whose power increasingly depended on firearms and organised hit squads, Mudaliar's influence was deeply tied to his local network.Several Tamil migrants were indebted to him and that he helped settle migrants in the slums of Antop Hill.His life later became the inspiration for Mani Ratnam's acclaimed film 'Nayakan', with Kamal Haasan playing a character based on the real-life don.Mudaliar died in Chennai in 1988.The Mumbai underworld of the 1960s and 1970s was not yet the sprawling international criminal network that would emerge later.The principal businesses were smuggling, gambling, bootlegging, extortion and control over illicit markets. Weapons were relatively less prominent.Former Mumbai police officer Rakesh Maria told TOI in 2009, that in the 1960s, common crimes included theft, pickpocketing, bootlegging and gambling, with knives and other traditional weapons being used.The growth of smuggling eventually created wealthier and more influential crime syndicates.The dons also had a presence in their communities that went beyond fear.Karim Lala donated to charitable causes, Varadarajan cultivated support among Tamil migrants and Mastan developed a reputation for helping the poor.This combination of crime, community influence and public generosity as a defining feature of that generation.That did not make them legitimate figures. It made their power more complicated.The transition from the old underworld to the new one can be traced through Dawood Ibrahim.Dawood had links with the older generation and had his “internship” under Karim Lala and Haji Mastan. But his rise was ultimately tied to a violent confrontation with Lala's network.The turning point came after Dawood's brother Shabir Kaskar was killed by members of the Pathan gang in 1981. A cycle of retaliatory killings followed.The violence eventually decimated the Pathan gang, with Karim Lala's brother Rahim Khan among those killed in 1986. Lala subsequently made peace with Dawood and withdrew from the underworld.The significance of that conflict went beyond one gang losing power.It marked the decline of the old Mumbai underworld and the emergence of a younger, more aggressive generation.Maria, told TOI, that the elimination of key Pathan gang members fundamentally changed the balance of power and helped create the conditions for Dawood's rise.Karim Lala died in 2002, bringing an end to one of the last figures of Mumbai's old-guard mafia. His death marked the end of an era when smuggling was the dominant cross-border activity associated with the city's gangsters.Haji Mastan had died in 1994, while Varadarajan Mudaliar died in 1988.Their legacies, however, survived in an unlikely place: Bollywood.Movies like, 'Zanjeer', 'Deewaar' and 'Nayakan' helped turn the city's real-life dons into cinematic archetypes — the imposing Pathan, the stylish smuggler and the feared yet benevolent local gangster.But behind cinema was a darker reality.These men built influence through criminal enterprises, intimidation and control of illicit markets. Their ability to command loyalty was often as important as their ability to inspire fear.And when their era ended, Mumbai's underworld did not disappear. It evolved.The local gang-leaders of the docks and neighbourhoods were eventually replaced by syndicates that were more organised, more violent and increasingly international.Before Dawood became the name most associated with Mumbai's underworld, there was already a generation of men who had shown the city what a crime boss could become.Karim Lala, Haji Mastan and Varadarajan Mudaliar were the 'dons' of that first era. Dawood was the gangster who transformed what came next.
Article Summary: Karim Lala, Haji Mastan and Varadarajan Mudaliar formed the old guard of Mumbai's underworld in the 1960s and 1970s. They controlled smuggling routes, gambling dens, illicit liquor networks and local rackets. Their influence extended beyond the criminal world into cinema, politics and local social networks.

Article Title: In space-starved Mumbai, padel finds room to play
Article Text:
The city has 150 padel courts spread across 40 venues.





MUMBAI: In a city where every square foot is fiercely contested, even recreation must learn to adapt. As Mumbai's playgrounds shrink and open spaces become increasingly scarce, padel is finding room to flourish. The fast-paced racquet sport that is a mix of tennis and squash, played on compact enclosed courts, is drawing a growing following among young professionals, fitness enthusiasts and groups looking for an activity that combines sport, socialising and leisure. As of now, there are about 400-500 padel courts set up across the country, with 150 courts across 40 venues in Mumbai.Easy to pick up, and less demanding on space than many traditional sports, padel is emerging as an unlikely answer to a question Mumbai has long grappled with: how do you play in a city running out of room?Ronak Daftary, the co-founder of Padel Park says, "Padel is like the coffee of sports. People are playing on weekday evenings. It becomes part of a routine. Instead of going out for a coffee with your friends, you are instead opting to meet over a game of padel."Being both an outdoor and indoor sport, finding locations to set up courts hasn't been all that difficult. At the heart of Powai's Hiranandani district, in their Business Park, a court has been set up. Lower Parel's Phoenix Palladium became India's largest integrated rooftop racquet sport hub."Padel is a sport where the court itself is the product. You're selling the sport addiction," says Daftary.Yet, not everyone sees padel's rise as an unequivocal success story. Urban planning critics argue that the sport's growing footprint also highlights deeper inequalities in access to recreation. While padel courts require less land than many traditional sports facilities, playing the sport often comes at a premium, with court rentals, memberships and equipment costs placing it beyond the reach of large sections of the city's population. Prerna Yadav from Urban Design Research Institute says, "Accessibility in sports is necessary when Mumbai already has land constraints".The sport's popularity reflects the increasing privatisation of leisure spaces in the city, where recreational opportunities are becoming concentrated among affluent neighbourhoods and upper-income groups. In a metropolis where millions still lack access to basic public playgrounds and open spaces, Yadav contends that the padel boom raises uncomfortable questions about who gets to play, and at what cost. "Because while a few might be able to afford going to a gymkhana to play padel, for those who can't, a playground becomes the space which can be accessed freely...irrespective of where they're coming from, they should be able to play any sport they want. It has to be a recreation space for everybody," she says.Ujwal Deole, the co-founder and COO of KheloMore, the sports venue booking platform, says the cost is a challenge which padel has to solve. "Padel has to be affordable. If it grows popular, many more people will also be willing to play". On the flip side, Deole also states that the cost of setting up a Padel court is high. "Padel infrastructure is close to Rs 20 lakh," he says, and hopes that schools adopt the sport to bring it to the mainstream.
Article Summary: As Mumbai's playgrounds shrink, padel is finding room to flourish. The fast- paced racquet sport is a mix of tennis and squash, played on compact enclosed courts. As of now, there are about 400-500 padel courts set up across the country.

Article Title: Wild boar meat seized in Sangli, pet dog killed because of explosive trap in Satara
Article Text:
Kolhapur:

The Sangli forest department took action against a 64-year-old man for illegally transporting wild boar meat in Bhashtewadi in Shirala taluka of Sangli district. Wild boar meat weighing 9.5 kg and a two-wheeler vehicle has been seized from the accused.The suspect has been identified as Tanaji Kisan Bhashte, a resident of Bhashtewadi of the Shirala taluka. A forest case has been registered and further legal action has been initiated.Range forest officer of Shirala, Ramesh Kamble said, “While patrolling the Bhashtewadi area on Thursday, Tanaji Bhashte was seen moving suspiciously on a two-wheeler. When our team stopped and inspected him, wild boar meat was found with him. Accordingly, the accused was arrested immediately. Hunting of wild animals, possessing its meat, captivity, sale or transportation is a serious crime as per the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972. ”The forest department has warned that strict action will be taken against those who hunt, sell or transport wildlife.In another incident from Satara, a pet dog was killed because of an explosive-laced meat ball trap, set in a field near Lohare village for hunting wild boars.There is an atmosphere of fear among the villagers, as explosive traps are being set at a distance from human settlements.The villagers have demanded that strict legal action be taken against those involved after finding out who set the trap. They have also demanded regular patrols in the fields near the village, monitoring of suspicious movements, and anti-poaching measures.Shyam Shinde, a local villager from Lohare village said, “Unknown persons had placed an explosive trap in a turmeric field near the village to hunt wild boars. However, my pet dog came into contact with the explosive-laced meat ball and it exploded, resulting in my pet’s death. The use of explosive traps to hunt wild boars is extremely serious, and such traps can cause grave harm to farmers, women, and the lives of school children. Today a mute animal was killed, who is responsible if a villager dies tomorrow?”
Article Summary: Wild boar meat weighing 9.5 kg and a two-wheeler vehicle has been seized from the accused. The suspect has been identified as Tanaji Kisan Bhashte, a resident of Bhashtewadi. A forest case has been registered and further legal action has been initiated.

Article Title: Maharashtra horror: Teen murdered, body dumped near Mini Seashore
Article Text:
A 19-year-old man was found murdered near a public garden in Vashi





NAVI MUMBAI: A 19-year-old boy was murdered and his body was dumped on the pavement near a public garden along Mini Seashore Road in Sector 10A, Vashi, early on Saturday morning. The Vashi police have registered a murder case against unidentified accused.Shashikant Chandekar, senior inspector of Vashi police station, said, "The murder victim was identified as Sujan Kumar Mahato, a resident of Sector 19, Koparkhairane. A passing pedestrian spotted him lying unconscious in a pool of blood on the pavement around 4am. The pedestrian alerted Vashi police station, and our police team reached the spot and took the teenager to NMMC Hospital in Vashi, where he was declared brought dead due to severe blood loss from grievous injuries to his head and wrist after being assaulted with some sharp lethal weapon. The victim Mahato hails from Bihar and resided with his father, who is an auto-rickshaw driver, his mother and two minor siblings. He worked at a roadside Chinese food stall in Koparkhairane and used to drive his father's auto-rickshaw during the night."Inspector Chandekar added, "Mahato had left home on Friday around 9pm, telling his mother that he was going to work at the Chinese food stall and was taking his father's auto-rickshaw to ferry passengers throughout the night.After his body was found early on Saturday morning, his family was informed. His father's auto-rickshaw was not found at the crime scene. Hence, it is suspected that after fatally assaulting Mahato, the assailant took away the auto-rickshaw, which is being traced by scanning CCTV footage along the route from Koparkhairane to Vashi."As there is no CCTV camera surveillance near the crime scene, we are scanning CCTV footage from roads leading to the crime spot where Mahato's body was dumped to zero in on the suspect. Mahato might have been fatally assaulted at the spot, or he might have been assaulted at another location and his body brought in a vehicle and dumped near Mini Seashore. Accordingly, using technical expertise, efforts are being made to detect the murder case. Meanwhile, Mahato's kin and friends are being questioned to get some lead on the unidentified accused."
Article Summary: A 19-year-old man was found murdered near a public garden in Vashi. The Vashi police have registered a murder case against unidentified accused. The victim was identified as Sujan Kumar Mahato, a resident of Sector 19, Koparkhairane.

The rescued youths aged 22-25 years were identified as Om Khilari, Parth Kadve and Rushil Vrindavan.





NAVI MUMBAI: Three youths from Kamothe who went trekking to Chanderi Fort near Panvel lost their way and got stranded before being rescued by the Panvel Taluka Police on Sunday.Gajanan Ghadge, Senior Inspector of Panvel Taluka Police Station, said that the rescued youths, aged between 22 and 25 years, were identified as Om Khilari, Parth Kadve and Rushil Vrindavan. They had started their trek at around 8 am.At around 11 am, the police helpline number 112 received a distress call from one of the trekkers, informing officials that they had lost their way while trekking towards Chanderi Fort."Upon receiving the information, we contacted the caller and asked him to share his live Google location. Accordingly, our police team, along with the Wavanje check-post beat marshal, Ritghar village head Deepak Patil, and the rescue team of NGO Sahyadri Pratishthan, launched a search operation by tracking the youth's mobile location," Ghadge said.The three youths were located within an hour in the hilly terrain and were safely brought down to the foothills.
Article Summary: Three youths from Kamothe who went trekking to Chanderi Fort near Panvel lost their way. They were rescued by the Panvel Taluka Police on Sunday. The youths were located within an hour in the hilly terrain and were safely brought down to the foothills.

Article Title: Navi Mumbai road rage: Ola driver attacked with stick, dragged 2km on car bonnet
Article Text:
The incident occured on the stretch of Sarsole village road in sector 20 near Nerul pond on Aug 15 around 9.35pm.





NAVI MUMBAI: In a road rage incident in Nerul after an argument between the drivers of an Ola cab and a Swift car as the latter claimed that the Ola cab driver had dangerously cut his way while overtaking on the internal road in Nerul on August 15 night, the Swift car driver assaulted the cab driver by punching on his nose and hitting on the head with a bamboo stick causing him severe injuries.As the cab driver bled profusely and attempted to stop the car driver from getting away till the cops arrived, by lying on the car's bonnet, the car driver drove with the cab driver on the bonnet for about 2 kms.The cab driver while recording the incident on his mobile in one hand and firmly holding the bonnet by other hand, shouted for help from passing motorists, while dangling dangerously and requesting the car driver to stop by yelling that he could fall and get killed.As the car slowed down after some distance, the cab driver jumped off the bonnet after which the car driver sped away leaving the cab driver injured on the road.The incident occured on the stretch in sector 20 near Nerul pond on August 15 around 9.35pm.Ajay Kamble, senior inspector of Nerul said, "As per the complaint by the injured cab driver identified as Pradeepkumar Pandey, 27, a resident of Naigaon (E), an FIR was registered at Nerul police station against the unidentified accused car driver, who is absconding.From the Swift car's registration number provided by the complainant, the accused driver was identified as Lalit Arjun Patil, a resident of Juinagar. ""We have invoked relevant BNS sections for the offences of voluntarily causing hurt/ grievous hurt using dangerous weapons or means, voluntarily causing simple hurt, rash or negligent driving on a public way in a manner that endangers human life or is likely to cause hurt or injury to any person and causing simple hurt to any person through a rash or negligent act that endangers human life or personal safety," inspector Kamble added.As per the FIR, on August 15 at 8.18pm, the complainant Pandey had picked up two women passengers from Andheri and dropped them at Seawoods Grand Central mall in Nerul at around 9.30pm.Thereafter, he headed towards Sarsole to attend birthday party of his cousin Nitin Pandey's brother-in-law Rahul Chaubey.Around 9.35pm, when he reached near Nerul pond in sector 20, suddenly a Swift car driver was repeatedly honking. Hence, he changed the lane and gave him way to go ahead.But, the car driver waylaid him and alighting from his car claimed that he had dangerously cut his way while overtaking and punched on his nose, while hurling expletives.As the complainant tried to convince him and told not to give bad words, the car driver went to his vehicle and taking out a bamboo stick, hit on his head causing severe bleeding.As the assailant sat in his car, the complainant tried to stop him, but he started his car. Hence, the complainant lied on the car's bonnet to prevent him from escaping till the cops arrived.The assailant drove with the complainant on the bonnet for about 2kms, reluctant to stop the car.After some distance, as the car slowed down, he jumped off the bonnet and the assailant sped away.The complainant returned to his cab and called his cousin Dipanshu Pandey, who took him to NMMC's Meenatai Thackeray hospital, Nerul.The doctors gave him first aid and for further treatment referred him to NMMC hospital in Vashi, where he was administered sutures to head injury, followed by CT scan.Thereafter, he lodged a police complaint.
Article Summary: The incident occured on the stretch of Sarsole village road in sector 20 near Nerul pond on Aug 15 around 9.35pm. The Swift car driver assaulted the cab driver by punching on his nose and hitting on the head with a bamboo stick causing him severe injuries. The cab driver attempted to stop the car driver from getting away till the cops arrived, by lying on the car's bonnet.

Article Title: Dhol-tasha troupes in Pune cover drums with bedsheets, mattresses to turn down the volume
Article Text:
Pune police are implementing a unique sound reduction strategy for dhol-tasha troupes.





PUNE: As the beats of dhol-tasha practice sessions grow louder with the festive season approaching, the Pune police have found an unusual but simple way to turn down the volume — asking troupes to cover their drums with bedsheets, light mattresses and jute bags.Following instructions from the Pune police, troupes practising in Sahakarnagar, Parvati, Aranyeshwar, Maharshinagar, Katraj and the old parts of the city are using these materials to suppress the sound without having to stop their practice sessions.“We had issued directives to dhol-tasha troupes to use blankets, jute bags and mattresses over the dhol so that the sound can be suppressed,” deputy commissioner of police (Zone II) Milind Mohite told TOI.“We do not want to halt their practice sessions, which help them hone their skills in playing these traditional musical instruments. However, elderly residents from Sahakarnagar, Parvati, Aranyeshwar, Maharshinagar and Katraj were calling the police control room every day to complain about the loud dhol-tasha beats,” Mohite said.“Every day, beat marshals used to visit these troupes and request them to stop practising or reduce the number of dhol being played.We then came up with the idea of reducing the sound of the instruments without hindering their practice. Since then, the number of calls made to the control room has reduced significantly,” Mohite said.A senior police officer said complaints were earlier particularly high during the evening and night hours. “Earlier, we used to receive around 100 calls a day, especially in the evening and at night. Some mandals used to play dhol-tasha till 10.30pm, while some continued beyond the permitted hours. Our teams would visit these sites and stop troupe members from playing,” he said.“The majority of dhol-tasha troupes are following our request and using techniques to reduce the sound of the dhol. They are using wet jute bags and mattresses, and the number of complaints has gone down,” deputy commissioner of police (Zone I) Krushikesh Rawale told TOI.“We have also requested them to display the slogan ‘Say No to Drugs’ on the dhol to spread awareness among youngsters,” Rawale said.Shirish Thite, treasurer of the Maharashtra Dhol-Tasha Mahasangh, said they held a meeting with the Pune police commissioner to discuss the issue.“We had a meeting with the Pune police commissioner, during which we discussed the issue of loud noise produced during practice sessions. We then urged our troupe members to use jute bags, mattresses or blankets to suppress the sound of the dhol,” he told TOI.The city has around 170 dhol-tasha pathak.“We have taken adequate precautions to avoid confrontations with affected residents. Our teams visit troupes that violate the practice timings of 6pm to 9.30pm and tell them to stop playing the instruments,” he said.“These are traditional instruments, and playing them is an art that requires practice,” Thite added.
Article Summary: Pune police are asking dhol-tasha troupes to cover their drums with bedsheets, light mattresses and jute bags. Elderly residents from Sahakarnagar, Parvati, Aranyeshwar, Maharshinagar and Katraj were calling the police control room every day to complain about the loud beats.

Article Title: 32-year-old man stabs his mother to death over alcohol
Article Text:
Representational image

Pune:





A 32-year-old man allegedly stabbed his mother (50) to death at their residence in Vishrantwadi around 9.30pm on Saturday.The incident happened following an argument. Rajendra Panhale, senior inspector of the Vishrantwadi police, said, “The man, who is unemployed, has been arrested for stabbing his mother to death. He was earlier receiving treatment for a mental health condition. He, however, had been doing well for the past two years, but became an alcoholic.”His mother, the officer said, worked as a maid.“On Saturday night, he demanded money from his mother to buy alcohol. He got enraged when she refused and he took a sharp knife from the kitchen and stabbed her in the neck,” he said.

Article Title: Techie found hanging in room, boyfriend booked for abetment to suicide
Article Text:
Crime

Pune:

TOI





A 23-year-old techie, working in a prominent IT company in Kharadi, was found hanging from a ceiling fan in her room around 1.30pm on Friday after she argued with her boyfriend, a resident of Paharganj in Delhi.Kharadi police on Saturday registered a case of abetment to suicide against him after the deceased woman’s father, a resident of Patna in Bihar , lodged a complaint.Senior inspector Sanjay Chavan of Kharadi police told, “The woman was staying in a studio apartment in Kharadi for the past two months. Her boyfriend is from Paharganj and works as a software engineer with a company based in Kharadi. After studying the circumstances, we can confirm that it is a case of suicide,” he said.The deceased and her boyfriend grew up together and attended school in Patna. Both secured admission to different engineering colleges and, after completing their studies, they started working. Both initially moved to Delhi, but the woman later shifted to Pune after securing a job as a software engineer with a multinational bank, Chavan said.“Her boyfriend came to Pune on Aug 20, and both were staying in the studio apartment.Though there is no suicide note, an examination of her phone records revealed that she had an argument with him over the amount of time she devoted to him. He claimed that she was not giving him enough time and was neglecting him,” he said.Chavan said that after the argument on Friday, he left the apartment and went downstairs while she remained alone inside, where she hanged herself from the ceiling fan. “Her boyfriend returned and alerted the neighbours and the police when he found her,” he added.
Article Summary: A 23-year-old techie, working in a prominent IT company in Kharadi, was found hanging from a ceiling fan in her room around 1.30pm on Friday. The deceased woman’s father, a resident of Patna in Bihar, lodged a complaint. Her boyfriend is from Paharganj and works as a software engineer with a company based inKharadi.

Article Title: Tears, hugs and relief as 100+ Nagpur pilgrims return from flood-hit Nepal
Article Text:
Family members welcoming Nepal returnees in Nagpur on Sunday

Nagpur:





After days of uncertainty, disrupted travel plans and a nerve-racking journey through flood-ravaged Nepal, more than 100 pilgrims from Nagpur finally returned home at 4.30am on Sunday, triggering emotional scenes of reunion at the railway station.Family members who had spent anxious days tracking developments from across the border gathered at the station long before the train arrived. As the exhausted pilgrims stepped onto the platform, they were greeted with hugs, tears and visible relief. Former mayor Dayashankar Tiwari welcomed several returnees with garlands and flowers, turning the arrival into an emotional homecoming.For many, the moment felt surreal. Asha Pandey, whose mobile phone was swept away during the floods, said the joy of seeing her loved ones again was overwhelming. “For four days I had no way to contact them, let alone see them. After everything we went through, being back with them feels like a blessing,” she said, struggling to hold back tears.The group’s troubles began to unfold on August 26 while they were visiting Sanga, near Kathmandu, home to one of the world’s tallest statues of Lord Mahadev. “We were supposed to spend the evening shopping afterwards, but the programme had to be cancelled,” recalled tourist Sushila Monde.“At first, I was disappointed. But once we realised the scale of the disaster around us, shopping was the last thing on our minds,” Monde told TOI.The travellers returned to their accommodation and prepared to leave Kathmandu the following morning as planned. On August 27, they checked out and set off towards India-Nepal border in two 45-seater Indian buses and an 18-seater vehicle.Their first attempt, however, ended abruptly. “Several stretches of the road were under water, while some portions had been badly damaged or completely washed away,” Monde said, adding, “Nepal authorities stopped our vehicles and instructed us to return to Kathmandu for our safety.”Having already checked out of their hotel, the group suddenly found itself stranded. Amid the uncertainty, traveller Yogesh Gawande stepped in to coordinate help. He contacted Nagpur MLA Pravin Datke, who escalated the matter to chief minister Devendra Fadnavis and a fresh evacuation plan was soon put in place.“The larger Indian vehicles could not continue on the damaged roads, so four smaller Nepal-registered vehicles were arranged,” Gawande said. “The local drivers knew the terrain well and were experienced in navigating the difficult conditions.”On the morning of August 28, at around 6am, the group set out once again. This time, the journey was slow and cautious as the convoy negotiated narrow roads, flood-affected stretches and challenging weather conditions on its way towards Janakpur.After spending nearly entire day on the road, the travellers reached Bhithamore checkpoint near Sitamarhi in Bihar around 4.30pm. “From the border, Indian vehicles took us to Sitamarhi, where the local administration and police helped us with medical check-ups, food and accommodation,” Gawande said. “We were finally able to rest and freshen up after days of hardship.”The group later travelled to Patna, arriving in the early hours before being accommodated for the night. On August 29, they boarded a train bound for Nagpur at around 7am. Nearly four days after their struggle began, the journey finally came to an end.When the train rolled into Nagpur before dawn on Sunday, the exhaustion of the previous days gave way to overwhelming relief. For worried families waiting on the platform, it was not just the arrival of a train. It was the return of their loved ones from an ordeal that few of them are likely to forget.
Article Summary: More than 100 pilgrims from Nagpur finally returned home at 4.30am on Sunday. Family members who had spent anxious days tracking developments from across the border gathered at the station long before the train arrived. Former mayor Dayashankar Tiwari welcomed several returnees with garlands and flowers, turning the arrival into an emotional homecoming.

Article Title: Chennai Bulls win equestrian champions league title in Coimbatore, bag ₹15 lakh
Article Text:
Coimbatore hosted the second edition of the competition from August 28 to 30

Coimbatore:





Chennai Bulls (Tamil Nadu) clinched the title at the national-level equestrian champions league, winning the top cash prize of ₹15 lakh at the event which concluded at Molapalayam near Vellanaipatti in Coimbatore district on Sunday.Bengaluru Knights finished runners-up and won ₹10 lakh, while Golconda Chargers secured third place and received ₹5 lakh. The final team scores were Chennai Bulls 311, Bengaluru Knights 291 and Golconda Chargers 286. A Raja , Nilgiris constituency MP,Coimbatore was the chief guest at the prize distribution and honoured the winners. Five state teams: Chennai Bulls (Tamil Nadu), Pegasus Sports (Kerala), Bengaluru Knights (Karnataka), Golconda Chargers (Telangana) and Elite Equestrians (West Bengal) took part in the event held in three categories: 100 cm, 110 cm and 120 cm.The second edition of the competition, organised by the Equine Sports India Federation, was held at a specially created show-jumping arena near ‘Beside the Power House’ premises. Revenue and disaster management minister K A Sengottaiyan, along with Sathyabama MLA and actors Arya and Shyam, had attended the opening on August 28. Sengottaiyan said the event reflected Coimbatore’s growth and called for more such events, adding that chief minister Vijay welcomed the championship being hosted in the city.
Article Summary: Chennai Bulls (Tamil Nadu) clinched the title at the national-level equestrian champions league. The event concluded at Molapalayam near Vellanaipatti in Coimbatore district on Sunday. Five state teams: Chennai Bulls, Pegasus Sports (Kerala), Bengaluru Knights (Karnataka), Golconda Chargers (Telangana) and Elite Equestrians (West Bengal) took part.

Article Title: National-level Equestrian Champions League show jumping begins in Coimbatore
Article Text:
Coimbatore:

The national-level Equestrian Champions League show jumping competition, organised by the Equine Sports India Federation; affiliated to the Equestrian Federation of India, began in Coimbatore on Friday. The event is being held at the Equine Dreams ground in Molapalayam near Vellanai Patti.Six teams representing six states are taking part in the league: Chennai Bulls (Tamil Nadu), Pegasus Sports (Kerala), Golconda Chargers (Telangana), Bengaluru Knights (Karnataka), Elite Equestrians (West Bengal) and Quantum Reigns (Goa). Each team has six riders and three substitutes, taking the total participation to 54 riders.Riders presented skill demonstrations and stunts during the opening ceremony, along with an introduction to the competition format, as horses cleared obstacles in the arena. Winners across categories will share a total prize purse of ₹30 lakh.Competitions will be held on three days till August 30, across three categories: 100 cm, 110 cm and 120 cm. The riders will be judged by Equestrian Federation of India-accredited judges based in New Delhi, while the course has been designed by a designer from Sharjah.The league was inaugurated by Sundar Ramakrishnan, managing trustee, SNR Trust; A S Sakti Balaji, president, Equine Sports India Federation; Dr R Mahendran, founder, Expovan; Dr R C M Vishnu Prabhu, ambassador for Trade, INDIA ASEAN Trade Council; and the owners of the participating teams.The final competition on Sunday is scheduled to be attended by K A Sengottaiyan, Tamil Nadu minister for revenue and disaster management; S Kamali, minister for animal husbandry; and MLAs N M Sukumar, Sathyabama and Tamilselvi. The prize distribution will be graced by actors Arya and Shaam.
Article Summary: The national-level Equestrian Champions League show jumping competition began in Coimbatore on Friday. The event is being held at the Equine Dreams ground in Molapalayam near Vellanai Patti. The league was inaugurated by Sundar Ramakrishnan, managing trustee, SNR Trust.

Article Title: Driver saves school children before dying of heart attack on Coimbatore railway overbridge
Article Text:
Representative image

COIMBATORE: A 69-year-old school van driver saved the lives of several children by safely halting his vehicle on a flyover here seconds before succumbing to a heart attack on Thursday.The driver, identified as S Shanmugasundaram of Mahakavi Nagar in Irugur, was transporting students home from a private matriculation higher secondary school near Singanallur.Around 4.30pm, while navigating the railway overbridge on the Irugur – Ondipudur Road, Shanmugasundaram suffered a severe chest pain. Recognising the immediate danger to the children, he managed to reduce the vehicle’s speed and manoeuvred the van towards the parapet of overbridge. The van came to a halt after a light impact with the parapet.Other motorists who witnessed the crash rushed to render aid, only to find the driver unresponsive. On being alerted, a 108 ambulance was sent to the spot. Ambulance medical personnel checked Shanmugasundaram and declared him dead.
Article Summary: The driver, identified as S Shanmugasundaram, was transporting students home from a private matriculation higher secondary school near Singanallur. Article Title: Erode woman burnt alive by man whom she befriended in social media
Article Text:
Representative image





ERODE: A 24-year-old woman was burnt alive in Erode on Wednesday by a man whom she had befriended on a social media platform.The deceased woman has been identified as S Vinodhini, who had been staying with her mother in Bharathi Nagar here after separating from her husband. She developed a friendship with Naveen alias Navaneethakrishnan, 26, of Sayalkudi in Ramanathapuram district.The Erode taluk police said the two had been in regular contact over the phone for several months. “On Wednesday, Naveen visited Vinodhini’s residence and confronted her over what he claimed was her reduced communication with him,” said a police officer. When the argument escalated, Naveen poured kerosene on Vinodhini and set her on fire. The man, who also suffered burn injuries, managed to flee the scene.Neighbours rushed Vinodhini to Erode Government Hospital where she succumbed to the severe burn injuries she had suffered.Meanwhile, Naveen got himself admitted to Amaravathi Government Hospital in Karur district.The Erode taluk police, who registered a case, had passed on information to their counterparts in neighbouring districts about the chances of the murder suspect, who suffered burn injuries, approaching a hospital. The Karur police, who came to know about Naveen getting admitted to Amaravathi Government Hospital, alerted the Erode taluk police on Thursday. A police team from Erode wet to Karur and arrested him. “He will be brought to Erode after his treatment is over,” the officer said.
Article Summary: S Vinodhini, 24, had been staying with her mother in Bharathi Nagar here after separating from her husband. She developed a friendship with Naveen alias Navaneethakrishnan, 26, of Sayalkudi in Ramanathapuram district.

Article Title: When you can watch cricket in stadium, why can’t appear in court, asks judge; orders health evaluation of Alagiri’s son by JIPMER team
Article Text:
Pointing out that former union minister M K Alagiri’s son Durai Dayanidhi is moving around and watching an IPL cricket match at a Chennai stadium and is also able to cast his vote with the help of others, a CBI court on Friday asked why he is not coming to court to answer the charges in a money-laundering case.

Madurai:





Pointing out that former union minister M K Alagiri’s son Durai Dayanidhi is moving around and watching an IPL cricket match at a Chennai stadium and is also able to cast his vote with the help of others, a CBI court on Friday asked why he is not coming to court to answer the charges in a money-laundering case.The second additional district court (CBI cases) in Madurai then referred him to JIPMER hospital in Puducherry for medical examination to determine his understanding capacity, soundness of mind and physical condition to defend his case.The court was hearing a petition filed by the Directorate of Enforcement seeking a direction to Durai Dayanidhi, an accused in a money-laundering case, to be examined by a medical board at AIIMS or JIPMER hospital in Puducherry to determine his present mental capacity to face criminal trial.The second additional district judge (CBI cases) in Madurai, S Shunmugavel, observed that the respondent had not completely denied that he did not go to M A Chidambaram stadium in Chennai to watch an IPL match between Chennai Super Kings and Delhi Capitals and also not completely denied that he had not cast his vote in the assembly elections. In his counter affidavit, he mentioned that he watched the cricket match with the help of others and that he also cast his vote during the assembly election.“If the respondent is moving and watching a cricket match in a stadium with the help of others and he is able to cast his vote with the help of others, why not the respondent coming to this court to answer the charge in this case? On seeing the activities of the respondent, especially attending to watch a cricket match at the stadium and going to cast his constitutional right of voting in the Tamil Nadu assembly election, the court feels that there is no impediment to go to medical test for his mental and physical ability to face the criminal trial before this court,” the judge observed.The judge said that the appearance of the respondent before the medical board is necessary to update his medical and physical condition for facing the trial. JIPMER hospital, Puducherry, is one of the reputed hospitals in India and it is run by Govt of India. There could be no influence by any of the parties to this case.The judge observed that the director of JIPMER hospital is required to form the medical team constituting a chief psychiatrist, a clinical psychologist and a chief neurologist and is required to submit the report from the medical team after getting the clinical examination as early as possible. “The director of JIPMER hospital, is requested to take a decision regarding the admission of the respondent/accused Durai Dayanidhi in the hospital, if necessary,” he said.After examining the respondent and after receiving the report from the medical board, the director of JIPMER hospital is required to send the report directly to the court in a sealed cover as early as possible. Further, the respondent is directed to appear before JIPMER hospital as soon as he receives the information for a medical test and co-operate, the judge directed.
Article Summary: Former union minister M K Alagiri’s son Durai Dayanidhi is moving around and watching an IPL cricket match at a Chennai stadium. A CBI court on Friday asked why he is not coming to court to answer the charges in a money-laundering case. The second additional district court in Madurai then referred him to JIPMER hospital in Puducherry for medical examination.

Article Title: A roaring Onam finale: Tigers take over Thrissur streets
Article Text:
Hundreds of ‘tigers’ throng Swaraj Round in Thrissur on Saturday for pulikali, a unique folk art event staged as part of the Onam celebrations

Thrissur

:





About 450 men, women, children and senior citizens, painted and dressed as ferocious big cats along with thousands of enthusiastic spectators took over the streets of Thrissur on Saturday as the city hosted another spectacular edition of pulikali (tiger dance), marking the culmination of this year’s Onam celebrations.The streets around Swaraj Round reverberated with the infectious beats of the chenda as the ‘tigers’ danced to the unique wild rhythm associated with folk performance. They bent low, sprang forward, swayed and leapt in energetic, feline movements, imitating prowling, stalking and pouncing tigers. The performance combines rhythm, physical endurance, dance and theatrical expression.Nine teams participated this year, a relatively high number compared to recent years. Each had roughly 50 ‘tigers’. Financial constraints had contributed to declining participation in recent years, but enhanced allocations from the central and state govts and the Thrissur corporation brought a significant change. The South Zone Cultural Centre also continued its assistance.A particularly refreshing feature of this year’s pulikali was the participation of women and children in a folk tradition where the rhythmic dance of pot-bellied men has long dominated the spectacle.One team was led by an eight-year-old boy and another by a 10-year-old girl, offering renewed hope for the survival and transmission of this vibrant folk art to a younger generation. Mother-daughter and father-son duos further enriched the celebrations, adding to the atmosphere of joy, togetherness, and community participation. The participation of transgender person Deepthi Kalyani as a tigress was another significant moment. The large presence of women among the spectators also reflected the festival’s growing inclusivity and appeal.The transformation of dancers into tigers remains one of the festival’s most fascinating aspects. Their bodies are painted in vivid yellow, orange and red, with bold black stripes and spots painstakingly applied to resemble a tiger’s coat. The process can take several hours, involving layers of paint, intricate patterns and detailed facial make-up that gives performers a fierce, exaggerated appearance. Some also wear elaborate tiger masks or headgear with ears and fangs.The chenda provides the powerful, penetrating beats, while accompanying cymbals build the musical momentum. As the rhythm accelerates, the dancers become increasingly animated, turning the procession into a dramatic combination of music, dance, physical theatre and spectacle. Each team also presented colourful tableaux and floats based on different themes, ranging from Mahatma Gandhi ’s message to Cockroach Janata Party’s protest.Minister for sports and youth welfare O J Janeesh flagged off the pulikali as the first team entered Swaraj Round.
Article Summary: Pulikali is a unique folk art event staged as part of the Onam celebrations. The performance combines rhythm, physical endurance, dance and theatrical expression. Nine teams participated this year, a relatively high number compared to recent years. Mother-daughter and father-son duos further enriched the celebrations.

Article Title: Hurricane threat in Southern California: 90% chance of disturbance to turn into depression
Article Text:
This satellite image shows Hurricane Karina strengthening off the southern tip of Baja California. (Photo: NOAA via AP)

Models show possible Southern California approach

Tropical storm landfalls rare in California

Karina reaches Category 3 ahead of forecast

Marine heat wave keeps coastal waters unusually warm

El Niño has more than 90% chance of becoming very strong

A tropical disturbance in the eastern Pacific now has a 90% chance of becoming a tropical depression within 48 hours, while weather models cited by Southern California meteorologists show it could strengthen into a hurricane later this week before weakening and potentially moving towards the region.The US National Hurricane Center (NHC) said the system, designated EP95 — its identifier for the eastern Pacific disturbance being monitored, was well offshore southwestern Mexico late Sunday and moving generally northwest at 10 to 15 mph. Its showers and thunderstorms remained disorganised, but conditions favoured further development.An earlier NHC outlook had put the 48-hour formation chance at 80% and the seven-day probability at 90%, figures cited by National Weather Service (NWS) meteorologist Bryan Lewis. The centre later raised the shorter-term probability to 90%.A tropical depression has maximum sustained winds of 38 mph or less. Under official NHC classifications, a tropical storm has winds of 39 to 73 mph, while hurricane strength begins at 74 mph."Once the depression forms, the National Hurricane Center will then likely write a discussion about it and include probabilities of tropical storm or even hurricane formation, so stay tuned for that," Lewis said.The NHC has not yet issued an official track or intensity forecast for EP95, meaning projections of a hurricane and a possible Southern California approach remain model scenarios rather than an official forecast.Kaj Goldberg, a meteorologist with KTLA, a Los Angeles television station, said forecasters were closely watching the disturbance. The station said weather prediction models showed a strong possibility of an eye developing off Baja California by Thursday, although the NHC has not forecast an eye forming at this stage. "This is the disturbance that, if it does form and come together, could make its way right into Southern California about one week from today," Goldberg said.He said the system could reach hurricane strength by Friday or Saturday before weakening by Saturday night or early Sunday. Under the scenario discussed by KTLA, it could then move farther north and make landfall in Southern California as a tropical storm.The station said such a track could bring heavy rain and extreme humidity into the following week, with flooding possible.The NWS is more cautious about those potential impacts. Lewis separately told the Los Angeles Times that there was still a high degree of uncertainty over whether the developing system would bring rain to Southern California, although higher surf and stronger rip currents were more likely over the Labor Day weekend.Direct tropical-storm landfalls from the Pacific are rare in California. An unnamed storm struck near Long Beach in 1939, while Hurricane Nora entered California as a tropical storm in 1997 after first making landfall in Mexico, according to the NWS. "However, several tropical systems have weakened below tropical storm strength before making landfall," Lewis said. "Most recently, Hilary brought significant rainfall and impacts to Southern California in August 2023. Hilary was not a tropical storm by the time it reached California."The NHC's final analysis found that Hilary lost its tropical characteristics over northern Baja California and became post-tropical before moving into Southern California. Despite weakening, it brought significant rainfall and flooding to the region.The disturbance is developing during an active period in the Pacific. KTLA reported that three storms were contributing to increased swells in Southern California, including Hurricane Karina, which was then a Category 1 storm and was forecast to potentially reach Category 3 by late Monday night or early Tuesday.Karina strengthened much faster. By Sunday evening it had become a Category 3 major hurricane with sustained winds of 125 mph while remaining far offshore and moving westwards. No coastal watches or warnings were in effect, though the NHC said its swells would generate dangerous surf and rip currents along southwestern Mexico and the Baja California Peninsula.The NWS separately warned of a high rip-current risk along Los Angeles County beaches. An earlier Sunday forecast listed surf of up to 6 feet and water temperatures as high as 76 degrees Fahrenheit, while a later update listed temperatures of 71 to 75 degrees.KTLA linked the potential storm to a "super" El Niño brewing in the Pacific and noted that the climate pattern is associated with warmer waters in the eastern Pacific.Citing NWS data, it reported sea surface temperatures across Southern California at 5 to 10 degrees above normal for the time of year, with readings of 74 to 76 degrees along Los Angeles County beaches.The relationship between El Niño and the current marine heat wave is more nuanced, however. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) has tracked a marine heat wave off central and Southern California since May 2025, before the present El Niño developed. NOAA says more recent warming off Southern California may increasingly reflect El Niño's influence.El Niño is characterised by unusually warm waters in the central and eastern tropical Pacific and can affect atmospheric circulation and tropical-cyclone activity.The Climate Prediction Center, part of the National Weather Service, says El Niño is strengthening and has a greater than 90% chance of becoming a "very strong event" during the Northern Hemisphere fall and winter of 2026-27.The climate pattern can influence conditions in which tropical cyclones develop, but it does not determine the path or strength of an individual storm.For EP95, the next significant development will be the start of NHC advisories if the disturbance becomes sufficiently organised. Those would provide official track and intensity forecasts and indicate whether the modelled Southern California scenario gains or loses support.
Article Summary: Tropical disturbance in the eastern Pacific now has a 90% chance of becoming a tropical depression within 48 hours. Weather models cited by Southern California meteorologists show it could strengthen into a hurricane later this week. Direct tropical-storm landfalls from the Pacific are rare in California.

Article Title: A man who grew up poor and fatherless and barely finished high school went on to open 54 Burger King restaurants across three US states; his foundation has since donated more than $2 million
Article Text:
Gullo got his start as a night manager at Burger King. Over the years he built up his business interests and eventually established a franchise empire in three states.

From success to philanthropy

A memoir built on life lessons

From heart surgery to pickleball pioneer

Gullo’s influence goes beyond business and philanthropy. In 2008, he had quintuple bypass surgery and then developed heart failure. He learned pickleball. The sport helped him lose 100 pounds and inspired him to grow pickleball in Northern Utah.

Service that connects people

An American dream to give

John Gullo’s story of overcoming a poor, fatherless childhood in a rough Italian neighborhood of Buffalo, New York to becoming a successful businessman and philanthropist is a true American success story. According to a Fox Business report, Gullo, now 82, built a career around Burger King, eventually opening 54 restaurants in Utah, Arizona and Wisconsin. His accomplishments included opening what is thought to be the first Burger King attached to a gas station, in Hurricane, Utah.But Gullo’s definition of success has never been about money. He grew up with very little and developed a belief that happiness, service and generosity were more meaningful than wealth. The report states that Gullo got his start as a night manager at Burger King. Over the years he built up his business interests and eventually established a franchise empire in three states. Later, he sold his restaurants, finding he missed working directly with young people and being involved in their development. The next chapter of his life soon focused on his passion for mentoring kids and giving back, adds the Fox Business report.In 2002, Gullo founded the American Dream Foundation, using his business success to benefit charitable causes. For the last 25 years, the foundation has donated more than $2 million to organizations and projects serving children, families, classrooms, firefighters and people with disabilities. Gullo has supported causes such as Prevent Child Abuse, the Children’s Justice Center, Enable Industries, the American Fallen Fire Memorial, Youth in Transition, the Ogden Police Department’s Let’s Play Program and the Treehouse Children’s Museum. The foundation also has helped fund the American Freedom Trail, which gives fifth-graders in Weber County, Utah, a chance to learn about American history and freedom.Gullo has documented his incredible story in his memoir, Extraordinary Adventures of an Ordinary Man, co-written with author, Bridget Cook-Burch. The book is a mingling of his life story with lessons to inspire young readers. Gullo has stressed the importance of learning from mistakes, taking action and seeing the opportunities life presents. All proceeds from the book are donated to charity, continuing Gullo’s long-standing commitment to giving back.Gullo’s influence goes beyond business and philanthropy. In 2008, he had quintuple bypass surgery and then developed heart failure. He learned pickleball. The sport helped him lose 100 pounds and inspired him to grow pickleball in Northern Utah. He helped build hundreds of courts, founded the Professional Pickleball Federation, and created the Tournament of Champions, including prize money he paid out of his own pocket. His work in the sport earned him a spot in the Pickleball Hall of Fame in 2024 and the Father of Professional Pickleball award.Gullo also has been working with former NBA player Thurl Bailey on charity initiatives over the past 20 years. Their friendship, despite their contrasting backgrounds and differing opinions, is symbolic of Gullo’s larger work to bring people and organizations together through service and community. He credits the Jaycees, a civic and leadership organization for young adults, with helping him overcome his introverted nature and teaching him valuable lessons on leadership, teamwork and community service.From poverty and a high school diploma barely attained, to building 54 restaurants, supporting numerous charities and helping transform pickleball, Gullo's life is proof of a belief that success is measured by more than financial achievement. Ultimately his story is about how one person can create opportunity for others. Having experienced poverty himself, Gullo has spent decades ensuring that children, families and communities have the support and opportunities he didn’t have. The American dream, to Gullo, was never just about making money. It was about building himself up and then using what he built to help others.
Article Summary: John Gullo grew up in a rough Italian neighborhood in Buffalo, New York. He built a career around Burger King, eventually opening 54 restaurants in Utah, Arizona and Wisconsin. In 2008, he had quintuple bypass surgery and then developed heart failure. The sport helped him lose 100 pounds and inspired him to grow pickleball in Northern Utah. In 2002, he founded the American Dream Foundation, using his business success to benefit charitable causes.

Article Title: In 2014, an American town was known as the 'food desert', but one man turned a college football field into a farm that generates 60,000 pounds of produce
Article Text:
A pipe dream

A resounding success

It has produced more than 50 varieties of vegetables totalling more than 30,000 pounds of produce.

Partnerships and future

Eight miles south of downtown Dallas, there lies an area that is federally recognised as a food desert, meaning there are no grocery stores or restaurants where fresh, nutritious food can be obtained for those devoid of the luxury of cars. This 95% minority, poverty-stricken area surrounds the rolling 146 acres of Paul Quinn College, a private, faith-based liberal arts college.Set in a valley on the northeast corner of campus, the field is everything you might expect at a tiny NAIA school. Bright white goalposts. A fading, antiquated scoreboard. A yellow and purple shack where fans can purchase tickets. And, tucked behind one end zone, a pair of navy blue blocking sledges for training. But there is no football practice happening on this ground, no whistles, no tackling drills and no sprints. All because no team calls this place home. Instead, the 20-yard line is occupied by bulging sweet potatoes, radishes, hens laying eggs and fresh tilapia swimming in a state-of-the-art aquaponics system, according to a report by ESPN.It was in 2007, that college President Michael Sorrell, a former college basketball player, decided to kill Paul Quinn's cash-strapped football program.Two years later, he transformed the old field into an organic farm. Yes, people said he was insane and his plan would fail, but 19 years on, the farm continues to produce."You know the Apple commercial 'Here's to the crazy ones?'" Sorrell said to the outlet back in 2014. "Well, that's us. We're proud to be the crazy ones. We weren't supposed to make it. No one thought this would work. But here we are. And I'm telling you, we think -- no, we know -- this is only the beginning. We are going to change the world with this farm."When Sorrell took the job at the college in fall 2007, it was in a financial crisis with a 1% graduation rate. He had no experience running a college, and had previously worked as a lawyer and White House special assistant. But he soon realised the healthy food scarcity the surrounding area faced. By spring, he had gained 15 pounds, thanks to lunch and dinner options that were limited to chicken shacks, convenience stores and fast food. The healthiest choice was Subway, three miles down the road.He was determined to make change and began talking with community leaders in the hope of getting a grocery store on or near campus. No one was interested, even when he offered free land. The words of his final prospective owner left a scathing mark. "He said to a friend of mine that the people in this neighbourhood don't look like his clients," Sorrell said. "And I just got furious at the injustice of it all. In the back of my mind, I may have thought that. But to hear someone say it, to have someone tell you that, basically, poor, black and brown people don't deserve what you provide? I was livid."That's when he had the idea to turn the field into a farm. He scrapped the football program, saving the university $600,000 a year. When the alumni of the program protested, he challenged them to raise $2 million to save football and none raised a dime.At a luncheon with a local entrepreneur who had been interested in community gardens, Sorrell suggested investing in the idea of farming on the field. The man said yes. Sorrell went to his board, insisting he had found the idea that was going to save the cash-strapped school, which had lost its accreditation a year earlier amid financial and academic concerns. "They said, 'It's going to make that much money?'" Sorrell recalled. "I said, 'No, it's going to serve notice as to who we are going to be. A voice for those without voices and hope for the hopeless. And if no one else wants to stand up for what's right, we will."He asked one of his employees, Elizabeth Wattley, to run the farm with absolutely no experience but an open mind. "I started reading books and Googling," Wattley said.Slowly but strongly, the farm succeeded. Through fundraising and a partnership with PepsiCo and its Food for Good initiative, a few training beds turned into the entire field. Students worked on the field as part of a work-study program that decreased their tuition. The farm became a cornerstone of the school's required social entrepreneurship program, which teaches students to become leaders and generate wealth through breaking the cycle of poverty and giving back to the community. And at minimum, 10 per cent of the farm's yield went back to the community it called home.Chanson Goodson, a member of the community, had grown up seeing posters of the football team around town but had never seen a game. Instead, when he roamed around, he would see children covered in dirt and wonder what they were doing. That is, until he became a student at Paul Quinn and took a work-study job at the farm for $10 an hour. "It was a job," he said. "Just a regular job. I would just go there and try to knock it out. I didn't want to touch dirt. I didn't want no bugs. If it was too cold, I didn't want to work. If it was too hot, I didn't want to work. It was a paycheck."But eventually, something happened. Goodson started planting vegetables, watering them, taking care of them and watching them grow. He started to show up for work early. Leave late. And take pride in the planting he had done. He pushed others to do the same. "I became absorbed in it," he said. "It became more of a responsibility than a job."Every semester, the faculty sees the same transition. The kids who don't want to be there and those who succeed. Soon, it transforms into a competition. "They're taking potatoes in the dorm. I've heard students in the dorm defending their tomatoes," Wattley said at the time.Sorrell believes it all comes back to a simple premise: the human desire to achieve. "When you are used to losing, winning seems a million miles away," he said. "What the farm does is, when you plant something, it grows. It's a simple and tangible example of your success. And you can't beat that."Since its creation in March 2010, the farm has been renamed the "WE Over Me" farm. It has produced more than 50 varieties of vegetables totalling more than 30,000 pounds of produce. It now includes a chicken coop, four active beehives and a greenhouse that houses an aquaponics system to raise tilapia. The farm sells directly to local restaurants and grocery stores as well as at farmers' markets. The farm's success has helped Paul Quinn restore its accreditation and build new partnerships with Yale, Duke and the University of Pennsylvania. The school has been named an HBCU of the Year. And Sorrell was named the HBCU President of the Year.In 2011, Wattley was watching the annual Dallas Cowboys Thanksgiving Day game when she nearly lost her mind. During a break in the action, cameras showed owner Jerry Jones looking down from his private suite as his Cowboys were beating the Miami Dolphins. He was nibbling on a radish. "That was our radish," Wattley said. "I'm sure that was the radish we harvested."Four years earlier, George Wasai, a football player in the 1980s at Bishop College, which used to occupy the campus where Paul Quinn is now, was among those fighting to keep the PQC football program alive. But when Sorrell turned the field into a farm, Wasai had an idea. He was the food and beverage director for the hospitality division of Legends, at the old Texas Stadium and at the newly constructed AT&T Stadium. Wasai mentioned the farm to one of his executive chefs, and a partnership was established.Now, an entire section of the farm is dedicated to the Cowboys. The team is Paul Quinn's largest client. Each year, Koski and Legends chefs work together to determine what high-value crops the stadium could use that will also help maximise the farm's revenue.According to a 2022 Penn University report, more than 60,000 pounds of produce are used in the dining halls and sold to local restaurants and grocery stores.The spirit of the game has not completely vanished from the field. The scoreboard with chipping paint still stands, the sledges are swallowed in bees and the light stands stand a bit crooked, all a reminder of what made way for what once was.
Article Summary: Former college basketball player Michael Sorrell decided to kill Paul Quinn's football program. Two years later, he transformed the old field into an organic farm. The farm has produced more than 50 varieties of vegetables totalling more than 30,000 pounds of produce.
